title: TRIM: Token-wise Attention-Derived Saliency for Data-Efficient Instruction Tuning
claim: Score data by deriving fine-grained token saliency from attention, building class fingerprints from targets, then matching candidates against them.
layout: 3 panels: left saliency derivation, right two stacked stages, left-to-right flow
description: The figure has three panels separated by dotted lines. Panel (a), on the left, shows a 4x4 attention heatmap for the tokens 'The brown fox jumps' in blue shades with numeric weights. Below it is a color-coded table (red, yellow and green) of row, column and aggregated saliency, with the aggregated row outlined in black. Panel (b), at top right, is Stage 1. A target sample passes up through a stack of decoder layers inside a rounded box. Arrows then lead to per-token hidden state and saliency pairs, and from there to a gray box of token-class fingerprints. Panel (c), at bottom right, is Stage 2. A candidate sample goes through the same model, its token states are scored by similarity to the fingerprints, and the scores are pooled into a pink 'Sample wise Candidate Scores' box. Tokens are color-coded consistently across all panels.
caption: Overview of TRIM. (a) From multi-layer attention, we derive an aggregated token saliency signal that combines row (allocation sharpness) and column (received attention) signals. (b) Using a small target set, we compute one fingerprint per token class by saliency-weighted averaging of last-layer hidden states, capturing task-defining patterns ([ref]). (c) For each candidate sample, token states are matched to their class fingerprints (cosine similarity), and token scores are pooled into a single relevance score for ranking ([ref]); top-ranked samples form the instruction-tuning coreset.
abstract: Instruction tuning is essential for aligning large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks and commonly relies on large, diverse corpora. However, small, high-quality subsets, known as coresets, can deliver comparable or superior results, though curating them remains challenging. Existing methods often rely on coarse, sample-level signals like gradients, an approach that is computationally expensive and overlooks fine-grained features. To address this, we introduce TRIM (Token Relevance via Interpretable Multi-layer Attention), a forward-only, token-centric framework. Instead of using gradients, TRIM operates by matching underlying representational patterns identified via attention-based "fingerprints" from a handful of target samples. Such an approach makes TRIM highly efficient and uniquely sensitive to the structural features that define a task. Coresets selected by our method consistently outperform state-of-the-art baselines by up to 9% on downstream tasks and even surpass the performance of full-data fine-tuning in some settings. By avoiding expensive backward passes, TRIM achieves this at a fraction of the computational cost. These findings establish TRIM as a scalable and efficient alternative for building high-quality instruction-tuning datasets.
